'''Jack Richard Norton''' (born May 5, 1945) is an American [[organometallic]] chemist and Professor at [[Columbia University]]. His research has focused on the studying the reactivity and properties of [[transition metal hydride]]s.  He coauthored the textbook "Principles and Applications of Organotransition Metal Chemistry."<ref>Collman, J. P., Hegedus, L. S., Norton, J. R., Finke, R. G., "Principles and Applications of Organotransition Metal Chemistry," University Science Books: Mill Valley, 1987. {{ISBN|9780935702514}}</ref>

==Education and career==
Norton was born in [[Dallas, Texas]] in 1945. He received his B.A. from [[Harvard University]] in 1967 and was awarded his Ph.D. at [[Stanford]] in 1972 under the mentorship of [[James P. Collman]]. After a postdoctoral appointment with [[Jack Lewis, Baron Lewis of Newnham|Jack Lewis]], he was appointed assistant professor at [[Princeton University]]. He moved to [[Colorado State University]] in 1979, and again to [[Columbia University]] in 1997, where he remains Professor of Chemistry. From 1992-2003 he was an associate editor of [[Journal of the American Chemical Society]]

His laboratory demonstrated the possibility of dinuclear reductive elimination from transition metal alkyls and hydrides by comparing the mechanisms of reductive elimination from (H)<sub>2</sub>Os(CO)<sub>4</sub>, (H)(CH<sub>3</sub>)Os(CO)<sub>4</sub>, and (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>Os(CO)<sub>4</sub>. His group later reported some of the first detailed pK<sub>a</sub> measurements of metal hydrides and demonstrated that the rates of protonation at transition metals can be quite slow.<ref>Kramarz, K. W., Norton, J. R., "Slow Proton Transfer Reactions in Organometallic and Bioinorganic Chemistry", Prog. Inorg. Chem. 1994, volume 42, 1. {{doi|10.1002/9780470166437.ch1}}</ref>  His group has also reported on the use of metal-hydride bonds as [[radical initiator]]s of cyclization reactions.<ref>Kuo, J.L., Hartung, J., Han, A., Norton, J.R., "Direct Generation of Oxygen-Stabilized Radicals by H· Transfer from Transition Metal Hydrides", JACS 2015, volume 137, 3. {{doi|10.1021/ja511883b}}</ref>

In 2005 he received the [[American Chemical Society|ACS]] Award for Organometallic Chemistry<ref>[https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/acs-award-in-organometallic-chemistry.html ACS Award in Organometallic chemistry]</ref> and in 2013 the Cope Scholar Award <ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.columbia.edu/cu/chemistry/ance/norton-cope-2012/ance.html|title = News &#124; Chemistry}}</ref>
